# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

When a heat wave strikes, the temperature a person actually experiences depends less on the regional weather forecast than on where, exactly, within a city they happen to be standing. A tree-lined street in Portland, Oregon, might be fifteen degrees cooler than a nearby parking lot. A dark asphalt playground in the Bronx can reach 140 degrees Fahrenheit at its surface, while a white roof across the street stays closer to the ambient air temperature. This variation is not accidental; it is the accumulated result of design choices made over decades. Cities that suffer in summer do so partly because they were built in ways that amplify heat, and the encouraging corollary is that cities can be rebuilt—or at least retrofitted—to do the opposite. The tools available are well understood: trees, street design, housing, and public transit. What is harder, and more interesting, is the set of tradeoffs these tools impose, because cooling a city is not free, and the costs and benefits are not distributed evenly.
